create.name: Chris Niebauer
create.bio:
Chris Niebauer is a cognitive neuropsychologist and university professor who writes about the meeting point of brain science and Buddhist and Taoist thought. He earned his doctorate at the University of Toledo, where his research focused on how the left and right halves of the brain differ, and he now teaches at Slippery Rock University in Pennsylvania, with courses on consciousness, mindfulness, hemispheric differences and artificial intelligence. He says the overlap between Eastern teachings and laboratory findings first struck him as a graduate student in the early 1990s, long before the subject became popular.

His best-known book, No Self, No Problem, argues that the sense of a separate self is something the left side of the brain constructs, and that seeing through it, much as the Buddhist teaching of anatta suggests, can ease a great deal of needless suffering. A companion workbook of exercises followed, and his newer book, The Abstract Mind, looks at how abstract thinking pulls attention away from direct experience. He posts short talks and exercises on his YouTube channel and is a frequent guest on podcasts and interview channels about non-duality and consciousness.

books.title: No Self, No Problem: How Neuropsychology Is Catching Up to Buddhism
books.author: Chris Niebauer
books.description: His first book for general readers, published by Hierophant in 2019. It sets research on the divided brain beside the Buddhist idea of no self and includes exercises for noticing the thinking mind at work.

books.title: The No Self, No Problem Workbook: Exercises & Practices to Help You Lose Your Mind
books.author: Chris Niebauer
books.description: A practical companion to the first book. Its exercises walk the reader through spotting thought loops and resting in awareness instead.

books.title: The Abstract Mind: How Thinking Became the Source of Suffering, and How to Break Free
books.author: Chris Niebauer
books.description: His 2026 book on abstraction as both a human gift and a trap. He explains how labels and mental models come between us and lived experience, with practices for returning to the present.
